There is one way to achieve it, you can use **.gitattributes** files and you can define in that file those folders/files that you want composer to ignore at the time when someone requires the library in the project. 
Like e.g. if you add the following line in **.gitattributes** file:
`tests           export-ignore`
It will ignore the **tests** folder and all those files/folders mentioned in the file will be a part of your library source code but those won't be included by composer at the time user downloads the library.

It'll be great if composer natively supported sub packages.

    require { "foo-vendor/foo-package/sub-package": "^1.0" }

...and foo-package's composer could look like:

    subpackages: ["packages/*"]

This would make both mono repositories and large projects split into smaller modules easier to maintain.

@chascode allowing multiple `/` in a package name would cause conflicts in the vendor folder when having to install both `foo/bar` and `foo/bar/baz`, as one package would end up being written inside the install path of another one. There a good reason why composer enforces having exactly 1 `/` and npm enforces having either no `/` with a name not starting with `@` or a single `/` with the namespace starting with `@` (which guarantees no conflict between the namespace folder and unnamespaced packages).

Supporting mono-repos as the source of packages is a separate thing (there is nothing forcing to use multiple `/` for package names handled in a mono-repo). packagist.org does not support mono-repos because it relies on the archives generated by GitHub, and GitHub does not support generating an archive for a sub-path of a git repo.
Private Packagist supports mono-repos directly because it can solve that issue thanks to the fact that it is hosting its own code archives.
Note that packagist.org is unlikely to move to hosting archives instead of using the GitHub (or GitLab) archives because that would require a huge amount of bandwith and storage, for which the project probably does not have the resources.

@stof I see what you're saying.

Instead of `foo/bar/baz`, maybe `foo/bar#baz`.  Since `#` is currently an illegal character in package names there shouldn't be any backward compatibility issues.

For namespace conflicts:

    <project root>/vendor/foo/bar
    <project root>/vendor/foo/bar#baz

I was imagining the composer client itself handles sub packages:

1. Fetch package meta from packagist (as it currently does).
2. Use git's sparse checkout to only download file content as and when required.
3. Sync files from `~/.cache/composer` to project accordingly.

There's still a few more problems to solve but that's the gist of my idea.

@chascode `#` is not allowed in URLs without encoding, which would be a mess for URLs to load metadata.
And anyway, we don't need an automatic convention anyway. Your packages can have an explicit name in their composer.json.

> 2\. Use git's sparse checkout to only download file content as and when required.

this does not work for any of the existing supported installation method of composer:

- installing from source keeps the `.git` folder in the vendor folder, which is useful when you want to hack development on your dependency. this requires having the structure of the whole git repo, not just a subpath
- installing from dist expects to download an archive (that is cached as is), which is the default behavior because downloading an archive is a lot faster than cloning a git repo (even for a sparse checkout, as this still fetches the git history)

So this would be a huge project.
[`vtsykun/packeton`](https://github.com/vtsykun/packeton) is a clone of packagist and does support monorepos. I don't see any reason why this can't be implemented.
